10592-adventures-in-friendship:
David Grayson, writing from a farm in the American countryside, made Adventures in Friendship from short essays about neighbors, visitors, and daily life. The book opens with a salesman who greets him like a brother because of lodge badges, then wonders what real fellowship means when it is not bought by membership. Grayson's voice is warm, plain, and gently humorous.

Later chapters follow other small adventures: talks on the road, kindnesses exchanged, and lessons learned from ordinary people. The theme throughout is that friendship grows from attention and honesty, not from clubs or ceremony. Readers looking for quiet, thoughtful essays on getting along with others will find this book easy company.
10865-play-making-a-manual-of-craftsmans:
William Archer published Play-Making in 1912 as a manual of craftsmanship for dramatists. Archer stresses that the book is essentially new, though short passages from older articles are embedded in it. He draws examples from published plays readers can check, turning often to Shakespeare and Ibsen as the most accessible playwrights.

More than half the chapters were written on shipboard and in places with few books at hand, yet the manual is thorough on plot, character, and dialogue. Archer's advice is practical, not theoretical. Aspiring playwrights get a classic guide, still respected for its clarity about how plays are built.
11045-the-ghost-ship:
Richard Middleton collected ghost stories in this volume, most first printed in The Century, English Review, Vanity Fair, and The Academy. The title story is told by a Fairfield villager, who calls his home the ghostiest place in England. Ghosts of lads who died in war keep tryst with lasses in the churchyard on Saturday nights.

Middleton's narrator insists that spirits stay where they are left alone, and that Londoners, curious and interfering, would drive them away. Other stories follow authors, critics, and villagers meeting the uncanny in quiet English settings. The collection charms through its dry humour and its belief that the supernatural belongs to ordinary places, accepted without fuss.
12730-the-high-school-boys-fishing-trip:
Dick and Co. head for the wilderness in this Gridley fishing tale, and find mystery along with trout. A strange packing box, left as a gift for Dick as trustee, sets off a hunt for its sender, while a haunting face and a captured camp deepen the puzzle. Rival boys Dodge and Bayless hover near the trouble.

The trip mixes camp life, a wild ride to safety, and a secret Tom Reade finally tells. Hancock keeps the tone light even when powder mills and night alarms loom. Young readers get outdoor fun with a detective thread, ending in the friends' usual loyal, laughing close.
12954-the-phantom-ship:
Captain Frederick Marryat's Phantom Ship, most notable of his three novels on a historic basis, tells of Philip Vanderdecken and the Flying Dutchman legend. Unlike its predecessor Snarleyyow, its ghosts are never explained away, and diablerie drives the romance in earnest, melodramatic spirit. Marryat's sea experience gives old Dutch seamanship a lifelike air.

A homecoming scene shows Father Mathias struggling to keep pace with Philip's strides, urging him to check joyful hopes lest disappointment crush them, as Flushing lies a quarter mile ahead. The novel blends sea adventure with supernatural dread. It remains Marryat's finest ghostly romance.
15381-victorian-short-stories-stories-of:
This volume gathers five Victorian short stories, all on courtship, by five different writers. William Schwenk Gilbert opens with Angela, an inverted love story told by a paralyzed man in a small room above a Venetian canal. He lives on thirty pounds a year, painting flowers and fruit in watercolor, with only a deaf old woman to tend him.

The other tales widen the theme. Anthony Trollope writes of a parson's daughter at Oxney Colne, Hubert Crackanthorpe of Anthony Garstin's courtship, George Egerton of a little grey glove, and Israel Zangwill of a woman beater. Love here is rarely smooth: money, pride, violence, and social rank all stand in the way. The set shows Victorian fiction testing how courtship really worked, beyond the romance of the wedding day.
1551-a-cathedral-courtship:
Kate Douglas Wiggin's Cathedral Courtship, first published in 1893 with illustrations by Clifford Carleton, follows an American girl touring English cathedrals who finds romance among choirs, cloisters, and close quarters. The courtship unfolds through cathedral towns, with humour, sentiment, and a traveller's eye for old stones.

Wiggin writes lightly and warmly, and the cathedral setting gives the love story a picturesque frame. The book went through many editions in its first year. It is a charming period romance for readers who love England, churches, and a gentle love story. The cathedral towns give the romance a lovely backdrop.
16273-the-manual-of-heraldry-fifth-editi:
The Manual of Heraldry, in a fifth edition from Arthur Hall in London, offers a concise description of every term used in the science, with a dictionary of every designation. Four hundred engravings on wood illustrate shields, charges, crowns, and coats, making the book useful at a glance. A transcriber's note records small spelling fixes, such as scarpe for scrape and seme forms in the dictionary.

Heraldry's language of blazon, tinctures, and bearings can baffle beginners, and this manual aims to make it plain and searchable. Antiquaries, artists, and family historians used such guides to read tombs, seals, and windows. The book remains a handy reference for anyone decoding a coat of arms.
16455-the-otterbein-hymnal-for-use-in-pu:
Edmund S. Lorenz prepared this hymnal for the Church of the United Brethren in Christ, ordered by its 1886 General Conference and issued in Dayton in 1892. Hymns are grouped by theme: praise, sanctuary, Sabbath, morning and evening, the Holy Spirit, sin and atonement, and the Christian life in all its stages. Later sections cover prayer, affliction, and faith.

The book was made for both church services and home singing, small enough for general use. Its order moves from worship through the life of Christ to the believer's daily walk. For historians of American hymnody, it shows what a late nineteenth-century congregation actually sang.
16921-plague-ship:
Andre Norton, writing as Andrew North, wrote this 1956 science fiction novel Plague Ship, copyright 1956. It opens on the Solar Queen, a Galactic Free Trader of Terra registry. Dane Thorson, cargo-master apprentice, stands in a cramped bather. Rip Shannon, assistant astrogator, rubs highly scented paste between his shoulder blades. The cabin reeks of spice, and Rip jokes that Dane will be the best-smelling Terran ever to set boot on Sargol.

Norton sends a free trader crew to Sargol, where talkative Salariki must be heard out before a straight answer comes. Trade, aliens, and a plague threat drive the tale. Readers who like classic space adventure will find a brisk, young-adult novel of a working starship crew, full of alien customs and frontier trade.
17266-the-banner-boy-scouts-or-the-strug:
George A. Warren's 1912 Banner Boy Scouts, or the Struggle for Leadership, opens with a roll call in a barn. Paul's troop must stay quiet, for Ted Slavin's rival crowd is out hunting them, and Bluff Shipley's stammer marks the fun. Chapters follow the disappearing coins, the first scout leader, a coward checked, Peleg's trap, the rival troops, a fire test, and a camp in the woods.

Warren writes in brisk boys'-book style, with pluck, woodcraft, and fair play at its heart. The Stanhope troop's road to the honor brand closes the tale. Young readers who like scout stories will enjoy a sturdy, old-style adventure of leadership earned, not claimed.
17414-the-blood-ship:
Norman Springer's 1922 Blood Ship opens with a writing man who talks so much that Captain Shreve spins his yarn just to shut him up. The passenger, weak of lung and hunting mild tropical breezes, seeks local color and news of King Waldon, the island trader dead in Samoa. Waldon sailed into a Samoan harbor in an open boat with only his beautiful young wife, and the captain knew him.

From that frame grows a South Seas tale of a cargo carrier, a vanished viking, and a romantic legend too good not to put in a book. Springer writes in salty, seafaring prose, with humor and mystery in turn. Readers who like sea yarns will enjoy a lively novel of the islands, their traders, and their ghosts.
19487-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
A. Hugh Fisher wrote this guide to Hereford Cathedral for Bell's cathedral series, published in London in the late eighteen hundreds. It traces the building's history, then walks the reader round its outside and through its inside, with a brief history of the bishop's see to close.

Old inscriptions get room here, including a bequest that freed travelers from tolls and a wife's proud approval of her husband's gift. Made for visitors who want sound facts in plain words, the guide still serves anyone walking Hereford's nave with open eyes.
19881-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
Bell's Cathedrals was a series of small guides to great English churches. This volume, by C. King Eley, describes Carlisle Cathedral's fabric. It adds a brief history of the episcopal see. The aim is a work both scholarly and usable. A student of archaeology should find it sound. An ordinary visitor or tourist should find it plain enough. That double audience shaped the whole series.

Carlisle's cathedral stands near the Scottish border, scarred by border wars. Its choir is among England's finest medieval works. A compact guide had to carry architecture and history together. Bell's series filled travelers' pockets across Britain. Eley's volume shows the formula working well. It is Edwardian heritage writing at its most useful.
20280-the-hill-a-romance-of-friendship:
Horace Annesley Vachell wrote The Hill, a romance of friendship at an English public school. Vachell assures a friend that boys like Verney and Scaife truly exist. No one knows that better than the friend himself, he writes. Chapters promise self-questioning, sacrifice, and a final good night.

The Hill opens with five hundred strange faces before a new boy. Life lies in front of him, and home behind, as he arrives. School tales of this era prize loyalty, games, and unspoken codes. Readers get a fond, serious portrait of friendship formed under school rules.
20651-a-jolly-fellowship:
Frank R. Stockton's A Jolly Fellowship, published in 1880, is a boys' adventure told by one of the boys himself. The narrator saw for himself everything worth seeing in the events he relates. He trusts his own eyes more than hearsay, and says so proudly at the start.

Will is a good-looking boy, with brown hair and gray eyes. He and his friend set out on travels that carry them far from home, into mishaps and discoveries. Stockton, soon famous for The Lady, or the Tiger?, writes here with the same dry fun, sized for young readers on the road.
20861-friendship:
Chasing friendship for gain is like chasing a rainbow's end for gold, says Friendship, from 1898. A true friend proves useful in the highest sense, the essay grants. Yet friends must never be billed like members of a dues club.

Hugh Black, a Scottish preacher, wrote this famed essay book on friendship's worth. He treats choice, keeping, and the joys and duties of true bonds. His warm, wise tone won readers on both sides of the Atlantic. The book stays in print in spirit, still quoted where friendship's deep value needs plain, kind words.
21067-overdue-the-story-of-a-missing-shi:
Clipper ships stood at their peak when Harry Collingwood set this tale of a missing ship, in the days before steamers ruled the seas. A seventeen-year-old midshipman of the Salamis is suddenly ordered aboard the Mercury, an emigrant ship found drifting in mid-ocean. All her officers have died in separate accidents.

The bosun and carpenter left aboard cannot navigate, so the boy must take command himself. For a while the ship runs well under his orders, until fresh trouble strikes. Collingwood, trained as a naval architect, writes the sails and deck work with authority, and sea humour runs through the danger.
21382-son-philip:
Philip Hexton, the hero of George Manville Fenn's novel Son Philip, is the son of an old mine owner. His parents hope he will choose a safer trade, but Philip wants only one job. He means to work as an overseer in the family mine, down among the men.

Under Philip the mine starts to run well, yet some miners break his safety rules on purpose. They smoke where gas may gather, and one man swears he will leave his mark on Philip. The story builds through tense scenes underground, escapes, and hard choices about duty. It ends with Philip running a mine that is both sound and safe.
21573-the-phantom-ship:
Captain Marryat retells the legend of the Flying Dutchman in The Phantom Ship, published in 1839, his thirteenth book. The tale opens in the mid-seventeenth century, on the edge of a small Dutch town. A cottage by a moat, with a narrow bridged crossing, sets the scene.

Philip Vanderdecken sails to free his father, doomed to beat round the Cape forever. A sacred relic, a loved wife, and dark powers bar his way. Judges have called the book one of Marryat's very best. Sea craft and ghost lore blend here in a way no writer has matched since.
21745-the-life-of-a-ship:
A small boy named Davy watches a new sailing ship take shape in a shipyard in this Ballantyne story for young readers. The vessel is the Fair Nancy, and her life from launch to wreck gives the book its plan. Davy is at last allowed to sail in her as a boy seaman. He is seasick first, then learns the rigging and the sails.

Storms strike hard: a hurricane knocks the ship over and her boats are lost. A raft saves a few, and a rope swum ashore saves the rest on a hostile coast. The crew walks out to a village and finds its way home by Quebec. The tale teaches how a ship lives and dies.
22107-wood-carving-design-and-workmanshi:
George Jack, a leading figure in the Arts and Crafts movement, wrote Wood Carving: Design and Workmanship. Jack had examined the methods used in working shops across the trade. He set aside vain survivals, the habits kept only because they were old. His aim is a standard of quality for craft work joined to design.

The book treats design as part of workmanship, not decoration added later. Tools, timber, pattern, and the carver's training all come under review. Jack wrote for students in the new art schools and for working carvers alike. His volume belongs to the movement that tried to save hand skill from the factory, and it still guides carvers today.
22541-the-misplaced-battleship:
The Misplaced Battleship is a comic science fiction story with a huge ship. Its narrator confirms a guess about the vessel late at night. It is a late Empire battleship of the Warlord class.

Undoubtedly, he says, it is a most efficient engine of destruction. Over a half mile of defensive screens and armament fill her. She could probably turn any existing fleet into radioactive ash. Misplacing such a ship is thus more than a clerical error. The story mines that absurd gap for humor and trouble. Bureaucracy meets doomsday hardware in its pages with dry effect. Readers get space opera played for laughs, in Harry Harrison's vein.
22652-a-campfire-girl-s-test-of-friendsh:
Jane L. Stewart wrote A Camp Fire Girl's Test of Friendship, a girls' series novel built around the Camp Fire Girls, the outdoor organization founded just before the First World War. The catalog record gives no year. Stewart's heroines camp, work, and face small trials of loyalty under the movement's ideals of health and helpfulness.

In the sample, Bessie looks back on a stay nearly spoiled by the girls in the camp next door. If those girls had had their way, she says, the troop would have kept not one pleasant memory of the place. Rivalry between camps, and friendship tested inside the troop, drive the plot. Such books taught outdoor skills inside a story, and they preserve the hopes adults held for girls of the era.
23111-riley-songs-of-friendship:
James Whitcomb Riley thanks his readers in Riley Songs of Friendship, dated 1885 in this edition. Riley addresses friends whose kindness reaches him only in ink and pen. Could he ever tell them the good they do him, he writes, speech would fail him into baby talk, his warmed blood laughing through his veins.

Riley, Indiana's Hoosier poet, built a national audience on dialect verse and sentiment, and friendship was his home subject. The songs gathered here trade in letters, reunions, and old neighbors remembered kindly. His lines were built for recitation, warm in the mouth and easy to memorize. Modern readers meet a poet America once knew by heart, preserved in one of his gentlest collections.
23154-the-hill-a-romance-of-friendship:
A platform farewell opens The Hill, a romance of friendship. A man and a boy pace a long station platform in silence. The boy wonders at his uncle's strange quiet. Then the elder John Verney stops, sets both hands on young John's shoulders, and looks down into eyes as grey and steady as his own.

Horace Annesley Vachell, to whom this school novel is credited, sets the boy's story at Harrow, on the hill of its title. Friendship between schoolboys, tested by honor, games, and loss, forms the book's famous core. A generation of readers wept over its central bond. Vachell wrote from inside the public-school world he depicts. The platform scene, an uncle's silence before a first term, tells new readers exactly what weather to expect.
24407-the-italian-cook-book-the-art-of-e:
Mrs. Maria Gentile compiled this Italian cook book, published by the Italian Book Company in 1919. Its subtitle promises the art of eating well, with practical recipes of the Italian cuisine, pastries, sweets, frozen delicacies, and syrups. The book opens with broth, or soup stock, the basis of nearly all Italian soups. Good broth puts meat in cold water and boils it slowly, with bones and soup greens: celery, carrots, and parsley.

Sugar browned at the fire and diluted in cold water browns the broth, and though broth has little nutritive power, it promotes digestion. A substantial broth for invalids cuts beef thin, covers it with cold water and salt, and seals the pan. It stays on a low fire six hours, then on a strong fire ten minutes. Soup of cappelletti, little hats, follows, with paste of eggs, flour, and salt. Readers get Italian cooking, plainly taught.
24576-an-interpretation-of-friends-worsh:
N. Jean Toomer wrote this short guide to Friends worship, published by the Friends General Conference at Philadelphia in 1947 at twenty-five cents. Its chapters cover worship and love, the basis of Friends worship and other inward practices, what to do in the meeting for worship, and questions and answers.

Toomer writes that worship is the action of the spirit, springing from our depths as love does. She explains silent meeting, inward prayer, and the place of ministry for newcomers. The guide is brief, plain, and welcoming. Readers curious about Quaker worship will find it a gentle and practical introduction.
24985-comedies-of-courtship:
Anthony Hope's 1896 collection, published by Charles Scribner's Sons, gathers six comedies of courtship. They are The Wheel of Love, The Lady of the Pool, The Curate of Poltons, A Three-Volume Novel, The Philosopher in the Apple Orchard, and The Decree of Duke Deodonato. Hope notes that four stories had already appeared without his consent, their titles changed beyond recognition, in a small American volume; here they appear in proper form by his authority.

The Wheel of Love opens on plighted lovers who should be happy: young, healthy, well off, with house, horses, river, and a weekly box from Mudie's. John stays with Miss Bussey to delight his fiancée Mary Travers, yet Mary sits sadly fingering a letter in her waistband while John strides moodily on the gravel. At dinner the party's cross-currents show: Charlie Ellerton's labored attentiveness to Mary, Miss Bussey's puzzled gravity, and Laing's calculating eye.
25493-a-cathedral-courtship:
Kate Douglas Wiggin tells a light romance that unfolds among English cathedrals, illustrated by Charles E. Brock. A young woman's tour of great churches supplies the setting, the company, and the slow chances for talk, misunderstanding, and growing affection that carry a courtship plot.

Wiggin, already known for Penelope's English, Irish, and Scottish experiences, writes in the same warm, observant voice here. Cathedral stone, music, and daily travel give the love story its shape, while humour keeps the sentiment from turning heavy. The Penelope books listed at the front show the same taste for travel talk and light comedy, now turned to a new romance.
26194-the-grain-ship:
Morgan Robertson's volume gathers ten sea and adventure stories first printed in magazines such as Harper's Monthly, The Smart Set, and The Popular Magazine. The title story opens in a restaurant. A white-haired commodore tells of a tight merchant ship found sailing the Bay of Biscay under topsails. She was deserted, with stores and water intact, yet her deck was covered with dead rats.

Other tales include From the Darkness and the Depths, Noah's Ark, The Finishing Touch, The Rock, and Extracts from Noah's Log. A later story strands a mate and a narrator at odds, armed against maddened sailors. Robertson, a lifelong student of nautical life, writes with salt-water detail and a taste for mystery at sea.
3005-tom-swift-and-his-airship:
Victor Appleton wrote Tom Swift and His Airship as a boys' adventure about a young inventor and his dirigible, the Red Cloud. Tom and Mr. Sharp build and test the craft, surviving an explosion, a collision with a tower, and a scramble off a roof. Andy tries a trick, a runaway auto causes trouble, and a prize gives the boys a goal.

The airship rises higher and higher, darts like a bird in huge circles, and comes to rest in the air when the gas machine fills its container. Later chapters bring a robbery charge, a wreck, a sheriff aboard, and a raid on a criminal camp. The book remains a brisk example of early science fiction for young readers, full of machines and chases.
30375-the-conflict-between-private-monop:
John Graham Brooks delivers a Weinstock Lecture on the morals of trade, published in December 1909 by Houghton Mifflin. As president of the National Consumers' League, he asks how private monopoly bears on good citizenship and on business life under a new economic order.

Brooks places the lecture in a series on moral law and trade, first given at the University of California, with companion talks on commercialism, journalism, and business in public life. He argues from the standpoint of consumers and citizens, not firms alone, weighing profit against public duty. The short book remains a clear statement of Progressive Era concern over concentrated power.
30379-field-trip:
Gene Hunter writes a time-travel story in which Kial, disgusted with a slow, cumbersome train, tries to learn the ways of strange creatures who are his ancestors. Lonely in a backward age, he spots a fellow being in the same carriage and hastens to introduce himself.

The stranger gives his origin as 8000, from the seventh galaxy, while Kial calls himself a country boy from the nineteenth way, only a period behind. Talk turns at once to the First Law of Thek, which bars divulging scientific or technical knowledge. Hunter uses that rule to stage a comic clash between curiosity, custom, and the future's regulated life.
32126-freudian-slip:
Franklin Abel's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in May 1952, opens on the day the Earth vanished. Herman Raye, a tall, serious, sensitive young man with an outsize jaw and red-brown hair, is standing in a mountain stream in upstate New York, fishing for trout. It is the last day of his vacation, sunny and still, with trout biting. Herman wears heavy black-rimmed spectacles because his patients expect it. His reading runs to books on personality, behaviour disorders, and self-esteem.

In his off hours, Herman also likes baseball, beer, and bebop. The story's question, posed in its tagline, is whether things are exactly what they seem, and whether life is real and earnest. When the Earth vanishes beneath a man on holiday, that question stops being abstract. Readers get a witty, unsettling tale about perception, profession, and reality itself.
32400-paper-and-printing-recipes-a-handy:
J. Sawtelle Ford's Paper and Printing Recipes, entered for copyright in 1883 in Chicago, offers nearly two hundred practical recipes for stationers, printers, binders, and kindred trades. The recipes, gathered from many sources and endorsed by leading workmen in the United States and Europe, cover problems that arise in every day's work. Writing inks lead the index, with recipes for white, purple, cardinal, portable, and indelible inks, and for removing ink from paper.

Printing inks follow, with advice on keeping coloured inks from hardening or skinning, preserving them, brightening common qualities, and making dryers. Invisible writing, copying ink without press or water, and hektograph ink also appear. The book gives a clear, hands-on picture of the print shop and stationery trade in the late nineteenth century.
32522-mr-spaceship:
Philip K. Dick's tale, printed in Imagination in January 1953, imagines a human brain-controlled spacecraft, promising mechanical perfection with an unforeseen result: a strange entity called Mr. Spaceship. Kramer and Gross face a living minefield in war, where board plates show pseudopodia, living shapes no mechanical system can beat, simple or intricate. The Johnson Control must be scrapped, and war sits at stalemate, with neither side able to break through.

Kramer argues that a living thing still acts from necessity, like inanimate material, but with subtler, more complex cause and effect. A brain in a ship, Dick suggests, may solve the minefield problem while raising a stranger one: what the ship itself wants. The story pairs wartime engineering with early Dick themes of mind, machine, and identity, in a compact, unsettling form.
32563-the-lost-warship:
Robert Moore Williams's The Lost Warship, printed in Amazing Stories in January 1943, opens in a lifeboat on a glassy, motionless sea. Craig rigs a piece of sail for shade and rations water at a quarter cup a day. He faces Margy Sharp, who begs for a whole cup. She argues that the two of them, tough where the others are not, could get along together.

No wind has blown for three days, and the survivors drift with no ship in sight. Williams builds the story from thirst, suspicion, and a strange blast that changed the fate of the warship Idaho, as Craig weighs who will live when rescue seems far away.
32615-the-hell-ship:
Ray Palmer's The Hell Ship, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in March 1952, opens at White Sands Space Port. There the liner Prescott settles into its blast pit from the Jupiter run. No hatch opens and no person leaves, while armed Company men board a ship whose pilot looks massive, black-furred, and inhuman.

Gene O'Neil, a newspaperman for the Galactic Press Service, watches from outside the electrified wire. His editor wants him inside White Sands, though earlier men who tried have vanished, and Palmer builds dread from secrecy, rumor, and a crew no outsider has ever met.
33605-the-girl-aviators-and-the-phantom-:
Margaret Burnham follows Peggy Prescott and her brother Roy, a seventeen-year-old builder of flying machines, in this girls' aviation adventure. Peggy rushes down the garden path waving a newspaper that promises ambitious young aviators their chance, and Roy, hammer in hand in his workshop shed, shares her excitement. The siblings are determined to make their mark in the air.

The story's phantom airship gives their flying a mystery to chase, as the young aviators test machines, face rivals, and learn the discipline of early flight. Burnham writes briskly for young readers, mixing family warmth with the thrill of a new technology. The book captures an era when aviation still belonged to daring amateurs working in backyard sheds.
3734-tom-swift-in-the-caves-of-ice-or-th:
Victor Appleton sends young inventor Tom Swift to the frozen north in this boys' adventure tale. Tom, helped by Ned and the faithful Mr Damon, builds and flies an airship after a map points to a valley of gold beyond the ice. Rival Andy Foger shadows them in his own triplane, and the race turns on storms, hail, musk oxen, and a rival claim jumped in the snow.

The middle chapters stage a wreck, a theft in the night, and a fight with native attackers, before the party reaches the caves of ice itself. Appleton writes at full tilt, with a new peril on nearly every page and a joke from Mr Damon to break the tension. Young readers who like machines, maps, and cold weather daring will find this one of the liveliest Tom Swift trips.
4608-tom-swift-in-captivity-or-a-daring-:
Victor Appleton opens Tom Swift in Captivity with Tom closing a book of adventures, yawning, and talking with his chum Ned Newton. A strange request from a circus man soon sends Tom off, with a warning to look out for a rival, alarming news, fire on board, and a narrow escape. Chapters follow a wild horse stampede, a living rope, a native battle, a desertion, and arrival in giant land, with a palace, a king, and a rival circus man.

Held captive, Tom uses a mysterious box, weak giants, a lone captive, a royal conspiracy, and twin giants to work toward freedom. The airship flight and Tom's giant close the tale. Readers get a lively boys' adventure of travel, giants, and invention, with humour and danger in equal measure, and with Tom's cool head turning a circus quest into a daring escape.
4913-chess-and-checkers-the-way-to-maste:
Edward Lasker's manual teaches chess and checkers together, moving from rules to mastery in clear stages. The chess half covers special terms, move symbols, and laws. Then come elementary tactics and fundamental endings. It weighs the value of the pieces and sets out general plans for king's pawn and queen's pawn openings and the middle game.

Illustrative games follow, including Lasker against Capablanca at New York in 1915 and against Showalter at Lexington in 1917, with problems for practice. The checkers half mirrors the plan, from rules to five fundamental positions. Players who want to improve get a structured course, not just a set of games.
6678-nonsenseorship:
G. G. Putnam gathers writers like Heywood Broun, Dorothy Parker, Ben Hecht, Alexander Woollcott, and the author of The Mirrors of Washington to mock bans on books and drink. The opening joke sets the tone: Haig and Haig costs twelve dollars a quart, while a booklegger can find Jurgen for fifteen, an economic case for nonsenseorship. Pictures by Ralph Barton add bite.

Essays on prohibitions, inhibitions, and illegalities follow, with wit aimed at censors of the 1920s. The tone is gay, sharp, and free, not solemn. Nonsenseorship is a lively period protest, fun for readers who like literary mischief and free-speech history.
7019-for-auld-lang-syne-a-book-of-friend:
Ray Woodward selects a book of friendship for Auld Lang Syne, dedicating it with affection to his father Fred Woodward. The introduction holds friendship essentially the same bond whether it joins persons of intellect and refined taste or those with little sense of their mission or duty. Its forms may differ wholly, yet the two friendships share points in common, drawing friends close in a bond praised through the ages.

No single philosopher's abstract theory can satisfy a reader on friendship's varied forms, Woodward argues. It proves interesting and profitable to note what various writers have said of this world wide force under past and present conditions. The book gathers those voices into a gift volume on an old and lasting tie.
8855-astral-worship:
J. H. Hill, a physician, opens Astral Worship with a demand for facts, quoting Boz. Then argues that much of religion, including Christian festivals, grew from worship of the sun and stars. Contents move from the geocentric system, earth, firmament, planets, constellations. Zodiac, through the sacred numbers seven and twelve and a twelve-thousand-year cycle, to the ancient triad, God Sol, ancient cosmogony, and the fall and redemption of man.

Incarnations of God Sol, the fable of the twelve labours. Anniversaries of solar worship follow: nativity, epiphany, Lent, passion week, resurrection and Easter, annunciation, ascension, assumption, the Lord's Supper, and even an autumnal crucifixion and Michaelmas. Hill's thesis, once popular in freethought circles, is now largely rejected by scholars, and readers should treat it as a period argument, not settled history. Even so, it is a vivid example of nineteenth-century mythic speculation.
9663-domnei-a-comedy-of-woman-worship:
James Branch Cabell wrote Domnei, a Comedy of Woman-Worship, in 1920, a romance of knights and ladies in Poictesme. Domnei, Cabell explains from troubadour lore, names a knight's service to his lady, proving love to merit love. Perion, unmasked and gay, woos Melicent, while a bishop aids him and Demetrios schemes. Parts follow Perion, Melicent, and Demetrios in turn.

Chapters trace wooing, wedding, oversea quests, and a final conquest, as love tests honor and wit. Cabell's prose stays ornate, ironic, and musical. A reader gets a rich medieval fantasy of love's service, half romance and half jest, from Cabell's invented province.
a-cathedral-courtship:
Kate Douglas Wiggin sends young Katharine Schuyler touring the cathedral towns of England with her aunt Celia, in a tale first published in London in 1893, as this edition's title page shows. Katharine writes the story herself in letters and diary notes, beginning at Winchester in May. Aunt Celia means to improve her mind; a young architect keeps crossing their path.

Winchester, Salisbury, Wells, and other cathedral cities pass in turn, with services, climbs, and teas between. The courtship grows quietly under the sightseeing, opposed by plans made for Katharine at home. Wiggin mixes travel notes with gentle romance, and the book became a favorite gift volume of its day.
adventures-in-friendship: David Grayson reflects on friendship as a lived practice, through neighbours, strangers, and old acquaintances met on the road and at home. Essays on fraternity, bread shared at table, and belonging show how small acts of kindness build lasting bonds. The tone is warm and unhurried, treating friendship less as an idea than as daily conduct, open doors, and time given freely.
astral-worship:
J. H. Hill, a medical doctor, wrote this study of ancient religion around one bold claim: the gods of old were the sun, planets, and stars in disguise. His contents lay out an earth-centred cosmos of firmament, zodiac, and constellations, then read sacred numbers seven and twelve as keys to myth. A twelve-thousand-year cycle frames the system's history.

Chapters name the sun as God Sol and retell the fall and redemption of man as a seasonal story. Feasts get solar readings throughout: the Nativity, Lent, Passion Week, Easter, and Michaelmas become anniversaries of the sun's yearly course. Hercules' twelve labours, hours, months, and seasons all join the pattern, making the book a full statement of nineteenth-century solar-myth theory.
bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-church-o:
A. Hugh Fisher wrote this description of Hereford Cathedral and its see for Bell's series, published by George Bell and Sons in 1898. The series' general preface states the bargain plainly: monographs accurate and well illustrated at a popular price. Each writer aims at enough scholarship for the student of archaeology and history, without language too technical for the ordinary visitor or tourist. A photochrom view of Hereford from the Wye fronts the volume.

Local benefactors speak in the text through old rhyme. One inscription thanks a man through whom all people may freely come and go. No custom, toll, or other woe is charged. His godly wife Anne enlarged the gift of house and land. The country is bound to pray for them, the verse insists, or else it were to blame. Fisher mixes such records with the fabric's measured history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-wor:
An entry on Christian worship, the homage paid to God, to Christ, to saints, and to things closely linked with God. Worship comes from the Saxon word for honour, the Latin cultus, and in its widest sense it covers hero worship, emperor worship, and devotion to angels, relics, and the Cross. This article treats Christian worship in its proper sense.

Degrees of worship matter most. Worship offered straight to God is latria, adoration due to God alone, since giving it to a creature would be idolatry. Worship of martyrs, angels, and saints is dulia, a lower, dependent honour for God's servants. The Virgin holds a rank apart, so her worship is hyperdulia. Even relics and images share in this dependent honour through their link with holy persons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-devil-worship:
An entry on devil worship, a pairing the writer calls hard to credit yet plainly real across ages and races. Worship and tribute work alike: subjects serve a just king gladly, but also pay blackmail to a pirate chief to buy off feared harm. Rude polytheism held both kinds at once, honouring kind gods in love while propitiating dreaded powers.

That fear-bought service, the entry argues, unlocks much of the puzzle, from African medicine men to medieval magicians. It also warns against a crueller error at home: crowds of innocent people were put to death on witchcraft charges. Quoting Augustine, it closes by suggesting that slander and cruelty can outdo any dark rite as devil worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-disparity-of-:
Disparity of worship is a bar to marriage set up by the Church to guard the sanctity of the sacrament. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that a Catholic may not marry a person unfit to receive the sacrament. That unfitness may lie in never having received baptism, the door to the other sacraments, or in denying that marriage is a sacrament at all.

It may also lie in denying the unity or lifelong bond of marriage, or in holding views that imperil the three ends and blessings of wedlock. The bar thus covers all who stand outside the Catholic faith and worship. The entry then works through the law in detail, a long study of how the Church shields marriage from unions that cannot bear its full meaning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-partnership:
Partnership means an unincorporated group of two or more persons, called partners, carrying on some set occupation together for profit, with profits shared among them. Lindley traces partner to part, to divide or share, and notes that co-partnership in the loose sense of co-ownership is now obsolete. English common law might still count an association a partnership even if profits served ends beyond the partners' own use.

Roman law treated partnership at length as societas, a consensual contract needing no form or writing, effective by bare consent. Archaeologists find it highly developed in ancient Babylon. Later pages sort its kinds, formation, partners' powers and liabilities, dissolution, and the canon-law questions it raises for clerics and religious, with English and Roman rules set side by side.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-relationship:
Relationship, carnal and spiritual, is the theologians' term for a connection between persons set up by nature or by civil or canon law. Three kinds are distinguished: natural, legal, and spiritual, though legal relationship lies outside this entry. Natural or carnal relationship springs from carnal intercourse of man and woman, marital or not, and takes two forms, consanguinity, blood kinship, and affinity, kinship by marriage.

Spiritual relationship comes from church law and attaches to Baptism and Confirmation. It runs between minister and recipient, and also between sponsors on one side and the recipient and his parents on the other. Under the discipline of the day it bars marriage between the persons named, acting as a diriment impediment, a barrier that makes a marriage invalid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-philli:
Robert Phillip was a Scottish priest who served as confessor to Queen Henrietta Maria in the troubled years before the Civil War. Ordained at Rome, he returned to Scotland in 1612. Betrayed by his own father and seized while saying Mass, he was tried at Edinburgh as a seminary priest in September 1613. His death sentence was commuted to banishment.

In France he joined the Oratory founded by Cardinal de Berulle. In 1628 he went to England as the queen's confessor. At her request he sought papal money against the king's enemies. When the talks were exposed he was impeached as a papal spy who had tried to pervert Prince Charles. Proceedings dropped after Richelieu objected to his name appearing. Phillip was later sent to the Tower for refusing the Anglican Bible oath in 1641. Freed through the queen, he followed her to The Hague and Paris, where he died in 1647.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-islip:
Simon Islip, Archbishop of Canterbury, was born at Islip near Oxford and died at Mayfield, Sussex, on 26 April 1366. Schooled at Oxford, he took doctorates in canon and civil law and was elected Fellow of Merton in 1307. His gifts as an ecclesiastical lawyer won him many benefices. He held the rectory of Easton, then exchanged it in 1332 for the archdeaconry of Stow, which he kept a single year, and held Horncastle rectory besides.

Bishop Burghersh of Lincoln, then treasurer and Chancellor of England, made him a Lincoln prebendary in 1327, and he held prebends in succession before becoming vicar-general in 1337. In London he entered royal service as a chaplain, and Edward III trusted him in diplomacy and politics, giving him wide powers during the king's absence in France in 1346. After plague claimed two successors to Canterbury, Islip was chosen archbishop in 1349 and ruled until his death.
chess-and-checkers-the-way-to-mastership:
Edward Lasker's Chess and Checkers: The Way to Mastership, printed in New York in 1918, teaches both games in one volume. Lasker promises complete instructions for the beginner and valuable suggestions for the advanced player. His preface notes that the world war had given chess great impetus. Prison camps, field hospitals, and trenches all played.

Part one covers chess: rules, elementary tactics, and the relative value of the pieces. General principles of strategy treat pawn openings and the middle game. Two illustrative games include Lasker against Capablanca at New York in 1915. Part two gives checkers the same treatment, with its five fundamental positions. Problems close each part. The book's diagrams appear as text drawings in this edition, and its tone is brisk, clear, and encouraging to learners.
doe-osti-17047520-evaluation-of-ethanol-: Ethanol in ships got evaluated, and this DOE report covers the marine fuel study. The pages weigh the green fuel at sea. The shippers get their answer. The fuel was evaluated. The answer was marine. The sea was weighed. The study was DOE's.
doe-osti-2584727-cog-software-architectu: COG's code got its blueprint, and this DOE doc maps the software's structure. The pages lay out the parts and links. The developers get their guide. The guide was architecture. The parts and links were laid out. The doc was DOE's.
doe-osti-3012259-human-factors-considera: People vs robot reactors got their DOE people-check, and this text weighs the human side. The pages detail the autonomy factors. The engineers get their data. The check was human factors. The side was human. The factors were human.
doe-osti-3374043-effect-of-magnetic-hyst: EIC RCS got hysteresis-effected, and this DOE text covers dipole fields. The pages detail the magnetic findings. The physicists get their data. The synchrotron was rapid cycling. The data were physicist. The EIC were field. The dipole were hysteresis.
doe-osti-3376627-solar-training-and-educ: Solar jobs are growing, but training doesn't reach every neighborhood. Kevin Finley's report covers a partnership bringing solar education to underserved populations. The program opens doors to clean-energy careers for people too often left out of them.
doe-osti-3377902-clean-cities-and-commun: Clean Cities got 2024-activity-reported, and this DOE partnership covers communities. The pages detail the report findings. The energy folks get their data. The report was activity. The data were energy. The 2024 were partnership. The activity were report. The cities were clean.
doe-osti-3398696-energy-technology-innov: ETIP got partnership-slid, and this DOE slides cover innovation partnerships. The pages detail the energy findings. The energy folks get their deck. The format was slides. The deck was energy. The ETIP were project. The innovation were partnerships. The slides were deck.
doe-osti-3484812-energy-technology-innov: Washington County got strategic-planned, and this DOE project covers Maine energy plans. The pages detail the energy findings. The energy folks get their data. The partnership was innovation. The data were energy. The Maine were County. The Washington were strategic.
for-auld-lang-syne-a-book-of-friendship:
Ray Woodward's For Auld Lang Syne is a book of friendship, gathering what various writers have said about that world-wide bond. Woodward dedicates the selections to his father, Fred E. Woodward, and argues that friendship stays the same bond at heart, whether it joins people of intellect or people with no sense of mission.

Its manifestations differ, Woodward notes, but friends in both cases are drawn close and united by a bond written about throughout the ages. No single volume could gather all that has been written on friendship, so Woodward presents selections that show its varied forms. Readers who enjoy anthologies of wise and tender writing will find this a warm companion.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIDisciplining:
A United Press article dated September 21, 1978 reports testimony before the House assassinations committee. Retired FBI inspector James H. Gale told the committee that the Bureau had secretly disciplined seventeen supervisors and inspectors. Their failure: they had not listed Lee Harvey Oswald as a national security risk before President Kennedy was killed.

Secret discipline meant the public never learned of the punishment at the time. Gale's testimony brought it out fifteen years later, during a fresh congressional inquiry. The article preserves that admission, a rare public sign that the Bureau itself judged its Oswald handling a failure.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TapesOwnership_: Richard Nixon gave sworn testimony after leaving the presidency, and the New York Times printed excerpts in August 1975. The questioning concerned the White House tapes and who owned them. Nixon's answers mattered because the tapes had driven the Watergate scandal and his resignation a year earlier. The excerpts let readers hear the former president defend his claims in a legal setting, under oath.
nasa-tm-19700029981-methods-for-nasa-uni:
A NASA task group on university relationships prepared this report in July 1970. NASA headquarters in Washington issued it. From its first days, the agency had drawn on universities for parts of the space program.

The report is a catalog, with commentary, of the methods NASA uses with universities. It also lists methods the agency and its centers could reasonably use. The ties run to administrators, faculties, and students alike. NASA asked for the survey as it tried to help strengthen the schools. In return, the schools added depth and skill to the national space effort.
nonsenseorship:
G. G. Putnam and others wrote Nonsenseorship, a set of sundry observations on prohibitions, inhibitions, and illegalities. G. P. Putnam edited the book, and Ralph Barton drew the pictures. Contributors include Heywood Brown, Ben Hecht, Dorothy Parker, and Alexander Woollcott. Frank Swinnerton and Wallace Irwin also appear.

The opening piece, We Have With Us Today, starts with bootleg prices. Good whisky costs less, it notes, than a banned book from a booklegger. A group of not too serious thinkers were asked for their views on pet prohibitions. No one of puritan leanings, the editor admits, was invited. Prohibition era America is mocked in essay after essay.
plague-ship:
Andre Norton, writing as Andrew North, published the science fiction novel Plague Ship in 1956. Its hero is Dane Thorson, cargo-master-apprentice aboard the Solar Queen. The ship is a Galactic Free Trader spacer with Terra registry. Dane serves under Captain Van, alongside assistant astrogator Rip Shannon.

Chapter one, headed Perfumed Planet, finds Dane in the ship's cramped bath cabin. Rip works scented paste into his back. The crew is landing on Sargol, whose people, the Salariki, will not talk business with a Terran who does not smell right. They can also talk for hours without giving a straight answer. Dane doubts the venture and says it holds a galaxy of ifs. Rip insists they will come out credit-happy if it works.
play-making-a-manual-of-craftsmanship:
William Archer's Play-Making: A Manual of Craftsmanship was published in London in 1912. Archer was a well-known theatre critic, and the book is his guide to how a play is built. He says in his opening note that the text is almost wholly new, and that his examples come from plays a student can read and check.

Early chapters take up the choice of a theme and the line between what is dramatic and what is not. Later parts turn to the daily routine of writing a play. Archer draws many of his lessons from Shakespeare and Ibsen, and the book is dedicated to Brander Matthews.
the-banner-boy-scouts-or-the-struggle-fo:
George A. Warren's scout story was copyrighted in 1912 and printed in the United States by Cupples and Leon. A meeting in a barn opens the contents, followed by a chapter on what it means to be a Boy Scout. Disappearing coins raise a puzzle early on.

The first scout leader is chosen, a coward is checked, and a boy named Peleg sets a trap that later turns against him. Rival troops appear, a fire breaks out, and a boy named Jack gets his chance. Headings such as Well Done, My Boy suggest tests of character as much as outdoor skill in this boys' series book.
the-blood-ship:
Norman Springer wrote a sea tale published by Grosset and Dunlap in a third edition, after a 1922 copyright by W. J. Watt. Chapter one says a talkative writer drew the story out of Captain Shreve. The writer came aboard that morning with an agent's letter, meaning to sail with the crew.

Weak lungs and a search for mild tropical air are his excuses; his real aim is King Waldon, a dead Samoan trader. He has heard Shreve knew Waldon, the island adventurer who sailed into a Samoan harbour in an open boat with his beautiful young wife, from nowhere. Shreve's yarn promises a bloody past behind that legend.
the-ghost-ship:
Richard Middleton wrote The Ghost-Ship as the title tale of a set of ghost stories, most first placed in journals like The Century and Vanity Fair. A villager of Fairfield tells the tale.

The teller grants that strangers call Fairfield pretty, while its folk find it plain but home. Fairfield, he claims, is the ghostiest place in all England. Ghost lads dead in war meet their girls on the green, ghost hounds hunt in packs, and a headless man sits by the well at noon while children play at his feet. The tale to come, he warns, was queer even for Fairfield, where the dead are part of daily life.
the-high-school-boys-fishing-trip:
H. Irving Hancock wrote The High School Boys' Fishing Trip, subtitled Dick & Co. in the Wilderness. The contents list chapters such as Tom Reade Has a Brand-New One, Dick & Co. Driven Up a Tree, Stalling the Red Smattach, The Box That Set Them Guessing, and The Scream That Started a Race. Chapter one opens on a warm night at a street corner.

Tom Reade, described as an amiable senior at Gridley High School, stops to wipe his face and neck and greets Timmy Finbrink. Timmy grants that the night is middling warm, though the heat does not seem to trouble him much. Hancock sets a summer outing tone before the wilderness trip begins.
the-manual-of-heraldry-fifth-edition-bei:
The Manual of Heraldry, in its fifth edition from Arthur Hall, Virtue and Company of London, promises a concise description of the terms of heraldry. It offers a dictionary of every designation in the science, illustrated by four hundred engravings on wood. Chapter one, on the origin of coats of arms, defines its subject first: heraldry teaches how armorial bearings and their accessories are blazoned, that is, set out in proper terms. The author declines to chase the exact period when heraldry began. Many volumes, he notes, have been written on its origin and on the antiquity of single charges in a shield, and an elementary work gains little from that inquiry.

In all ages and countries, he observes, men emerging from barbarism to civilization have used figures of living things as marks. The manual teaches a symbolic language through its dictionary and plates.
the-otterbein-hymnal-for-use-in-public-a: The Otterbein Hymnal was prepared by Edmund S. Lorenz for use in public and social worship, and published at Dayton, Ohio, in 1892 by the United Brethren Publishing House. The Church of the United Brethren in Christ had ordered a small hymnal for general church purposes in 1886. Only the front matter is present here, so the hymns themselves do not appear. The pages name the advisory committee on music and letters, and a table of contents begins but is cut off.
the-phantom-ship: Captain Frederick Marryat wrote The Phantom Ship, shown here in a London printing dated in roman numerals 1896. The title page and a bare contents list are all that is present, so the novel itself does not appear. The list names thirty-seven chapters by number alone, with no titles. A second record carries the same 1896 title page but a shorter contents list, and a third record, labeled part 2, carries the opening chapter instead.
tom-swift-and-his-airship:
Victor Appleton opens Tom Swift and His Airship with an explosion chapter in a laboratory. Tom stands ready by complicated apparatus while Mr. Sharp, a dark, nervous man, leans over a large tank and warns him to look out. Sharp is about to turn on the gas, unsure what may happen.

Contents promise a trial trip, colliding with a tower, getting off a roof, a runaway auto, and the Red Cloud departing. Later chapters bring robbery charges, a wreck, a sheriff aboard, and a raid. Readers get a boys' airship adventure that begins with a risky gas experiment.
tom-swift-in-captivity-or-a-daring-escap: A Daring Escape by Airship is promised in the Tom Swift in captivity story by Victor Appleton, presented through twenty-five chapter headings. A strange request and a circus man open the book, and Tom decides to go despite warnings about a rival. Fire on board and a narrow escape follow. Later headings bring a wild horse stampede, a native battle, giant land, a king's palace, captives held, and weak giants. Chapter one is announced without text following. The contents list alone is given in this record.
tom-swift-in-the-caves-of-ice-or-the-wre: Victor Appleton's Tom Swift in the Caves of Ice, or the Wreck of the Airship, is presented through twenty-five chapter headings. Andy Foger's triplane, a stolen map, and grave suspicions start the rivalry. Chapter one opens with Eradicate asking whether Tom will fly again today, and Tom planning a trip to Waterford to call on Mr. Damon, then breaks off. Later headings promise musk oxen, ice caves, a gold valley, a wreck, and rescue. The contents and that opening exchange are what is present here.
victorian-short-stories-stories-of-court:
Victorian Short Stories: Stories of Courtship gathers five tales of lovers. Angela, an inverted love story by William Schwenk Gilbert, leads the book. Anthony Trollope adds The Parson's Daughter of Oxney Colne. Hubert Crackanthorpe, George Egerton, and Israel Zangwill complete the set. Gilbert's tale is noted as first printed in The Century Magazine in September 1890.

His narrator is a poor paralysed man. For six years he has lived in one small room over a side canal in Venice. A deaf old woman tends him and makes his bed. He lives on some thirty pounds a year from watercolor drawings of flowers and fruit, sold in London through a friend. He describes his window with care. It stands five feet above the canal water, and the house juts out above it. That odd room drives his tale. Courtship here comes inverted indeed, watched from a sickbed.
